title: No one can purify another (161–166)
hook: by oneself evil is done, by oneself one is purified
carry: no one can do it for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, first yourself: set yourself right, then teach. Your line was self is lord of self. Did you practice one piece of your own advice? Day one hundred ninety.

Someone can drive you to the gym. They can buy you the shoes, set the alarm, even stand next to you on the treadmill cheering. But they cannot do your push-ups for you. If they do fifty, your arms stay exactly as they were. Everyone knows this about the body. We're less sure about it with the mind. We'd love for someone to hand us calm, or patience, or a clean conscience, already assembled. Chapter twelve ends with a verse that gently shuts that door. Today: no one can purify another.
screen: `THEY CAN DRIVE YOU TO THE GYM.` → `THEY CAN'T DO YOUR PUSH-UPS.` → `CALM, ALREADY ASSEMBLED?`

segments.voice: The chapter begins its ending with a warning. Verse one sixty-three, in Max Müller's words: "Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do." No sugarcoating. Just before that, verse one sixty-two pictures harm as a creeping vine that slowly strangles the tree it wraps around. Then the heart of it, verse one sixty-five: "By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another." The Pali word for purity is suddhi, the same root as clean, clear. The verse is careful and balanced: four lines, harm and its undoing, both in your own hands. That's sobering, and also freeing. If no one else can make you pure, no one else can make you impure either. Then verse one sixty-six, with a story. The commentary says that when the Buddha announced he would pass away in four months, many monks crowded around him anxiously. One monk, named Attadattha, stayed away and meditated instead. The others complained. When asked, he explained he wanted to reach the goal while the Buddha was still alive, and the Buddha praised him: this is how to honor me. Don't neglect your own good for another's, the verse says. It doesn't mean you walk alone. Teachers and friends matter enormously in Buddhism. But they're the ones driving you to the gym.
screen: `HARM IS EASY; GOOD IS HARD.` · `SUDDHI — PURITY.` · `BOTH IN YOUR OWN HANDS.` · `ATTADATTHA STAYS AND SITS.` · then, large: `NO ONE CAN DO IT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you've been waiting for someone else to fix in you. Maybe you're waiting to be less anxious once work calms down, or kinder once your family is easier. Hold it for a moment. Then ask: what is one step I can take myself, today, however small? Not the whole journey. One step. Once you've found it, let it rest, and do the one step that's already in your hands: this breath, then this one. The bell holds the time.
No one can purify another. Verse one sixty-five: by oneself harm is done, by oneself one is purified; purity and impurity are one's own.
screen: `NO ONE CAN PURIFY ANOTHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no one can do it for you. Today, take the one step you found, yourself, without waiting for anyone's permission or help. Day one hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Buddhists honor teachers, monastics and spiritual friends as essential guides, while holding, as this verse says, that each person must do the work of purifying their own mind.

fork.setup: the Buddha has said he'll pass away in four months. everyone crowds around him. you're Attadattha. what do you do?
options: go and meditate, to reach the goal while he's alive.
fork.reveal: he went to meditate. the others complained, but the Buddha praised him: that's how to honor the teacher.

original.note: Pali: purity, cleanness — the word in verse 165 for what no one can give another.

trapdoor: what you thought: you're on your own.
what it means: others can guide and help, but harm and its undoing are in your own hands.
what a scholar hears: verse 165's four lines balance doing and undoing, suffering and purification; the commentary ties verse 166 to Attadattha.
